utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Mr. Tolimir continues today his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to welcome the witness and everyone present in the courtroom. May this day in court and may the final judgement reflect God's will and not my will.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, could I call up in e-court P895. It is an autopsy report. We need page 2. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We are interested in the manner of determining the age of the person at the moment they died. In this report the age range for one person is determined as 35 to 60. This is probably an estimate made by an anthropologist, but can you give us, from a pathologist's perspective, your opinion as to why this range is so broad?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- you are correct that the estimation was done by the anthropologists and they did this by looking at the bone, certain parts of the bones, particularly the pelvis and maybe the ribs, and they know from tables and figures that that can give an indication of age range. Now, the younger a person is -- because they are still growing, the younger the person is, the easier it is to see more precisely how old they are. So as a young child you can practically tell almost to the year how old the person is. As you get older and particularly by the 20s, late 20s, et cetera, it becomes much or difficult and you start using broad age ranges. Above perhaps about 30, not much changes in your body, so somebody from a bone point of view, the bone could look the same as somebody who is 30 as somebody who is perhaps 60. As you get older and people develop arthritis and other diseases, then you can perhaps say that that is an older person, but that's not always predictable because younger people can get arthritis. So really what I'm saying is that the older you get, the more difficult it is to be precise. This is from simply looking at the bones and that is all we had here to look at. So their duty-bound to give a very wide age range. I think they would be the first to accept this person could be even slightly out with that, it could be 34, it could be 61, but it's somebody of middle age, it would appear, simply from looking at the bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. If that is indeed so, if this is a certain problem to determine the age range and you establish it as 35 to 60, is there any problem with older persons, could it happen that their age is determined as 80 instead of 60? How do you determine the age of older persons? What is the range that applies to them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, the same comments really apply and -- I'm aware that, I think, some people were said to be older from anthropological point of view, but I think subsequent inquiries have revealed they are actually younger. The trouble is that the anthropologists were basing their studies, this is on looking at the bones in the pelvis, et cetera, on research that's been done a number of years ago with a different population of people, not people from the Balkans. So there's a limitation, a limitation there already. So that's why I think they are being fair. They are giving a broad range of ages and, yes, it does become more difficult with the elderly people, they could actually be younger in reality than what they've estimated. I think at the other end, I think we are pretty safe in saying that somebody is a young person in the teens or thereabouts, that is a lot more -- it's possible to be a lot more precise about that because then you can look at the teeth as well, and teeth can give an indication of age. But so the younger it's easier; older, much more difficult. Can I just make one general observation for the Court that Mr. Tolimir refers to me as Professor. I am not actually a professor, but just -- I'm just Doctor, but just in case anybody misunderstood that title. It's in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Thank you, Professor. Can we -- can you tell us, while we are on the subject, what exactly is your job at the university?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At my own university in Glasgow I'm a forensic pathologist who carries out a large number of post-mortem examinations every year on people who have died suddenly. This would be people who have died of natural disease, from accidents, from suicides, from alcohol, from drugs, and homicides. It's a whole range of material. I also teach at the university and do other things. The system of professors in our country is different, I think, from other countries, so it may well be that in my position in your country, I would be a professor, but it's just we have a slightly different system in our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, I apologise for that. Doctor, since we've made an introduction for my next question, I want to ask you if there had been any pressure on you while you were doing this work to finish it by a certain dead-line or to apply a method that you perhaps did not agree with, something along those lines?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. We were aware that there was a limit to the time the mortuary could operate because just of physical conditions, of the weather and facilities, and this did, in fact, happen and the bodies were left -- for that grave were left over to the following year. So there was absolutely no pressure to abandon work, to take any shortcuts or to do anything of that sort. Absolutely not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any comments made on your written reports? Did anyone make any demands to have certain changes made in these reports or to put in different qualifications?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. None at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, and did you, Doctor, have a toxicologist on your team?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was there any information indicating that perhaps chemical weapons were used and did you find any traces of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were given no information about use of chemical weapons. I don't think it is something that we would have seen any evidence of. I've no experience of chemical weapons, but in terms of perhaps burning, well, we wouldn't have seen that anyway, but there was no -- that was never mentioned to us at all. I think it would have been -- even if it had, it would have been extremely difficult to -- if not impossible to detect any evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you, as chief pathologist, supervise the work and reports of other pathologists working in the mortuary? And were they perhaps susceptible to any other influence, along the lines I indicated in one of my previous questions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's two parts to that question. No, the other pathologists were under no influence whatsoever. They were entirely individual pathologists gathered from all different countries of the world. I was there all the time. Generally the pathologists came for shorter periods, so clearly they had less experience in this work than I eventually had. I was able to offer them guidance and as to how -- what things to expect, how to construct -- generally construct a report and what information we were looking for, and very quickly they built that up. But I think if you were to look at individual post-mortem reports from somebody from a European country, somebody from Egypt, from Sri Lanka, et cetera, you would find a different way of describing injuries which does, I think, emphasise their independence and their ability to put their own thoughts on the paper. There was certainly no pressure from myself or anyone else to point to them and tell, You've got to write that. They were given guidance about the general information we were looking for in the cases, and they compiled the reports, but no pressure at all. Often we would discuss difficult cases between us and anthropologists, we would all gather around the table and look at these things, and perhaps come to a consensus view.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Since there were less experienced and more experienced people and you were the chief, did you perhaps have occasion to modify the reports made by other pathologists if you noticed there were some errors, mistakes in them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. When reviewing the reports, as I reviewed all the reports, for the final reports, in going through them, I would notice perhaps they've got -- somebody got left and right incorrect, and with the benefit of photographs and other diagrams, I was able to correct them. And other simple errors like that I would correct, and I think that was my role to do that. But I didn't alter causes of death, and you can see we explained yesterday about the -- sometimes the difficulty in establishing the precise wording of cause of death, so because I have made no alterations to these, so I would have this slight -- slight perhaps confusion, but it's not, so no, I didn't -- other than basic grammatical and factual errors, I made no changes. Perhaps one slightly allied -- I think you'll see this in my final report for 2001, I've made a comment for some of the cases which at the time of the mortuary operations we labelled body parts. In my reviewing all the cases, I felt there was sufficient of body to make it -- body part to make it a body. That didn't alter in any way the gun-shot injuries or other findings on that, I just thought we had enough there to make it a body and another person. But it doesn't -- it certainly doesn't alter the basic pathology in that body or body part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us now, since you were the chief of that team that you supervised, to whom you gave assignments, were you answerable for your work to some superior to whom you possibly submitted interim reports in this work?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly I was being asked to produce a report for the Tribunal here. I worked through investigators for individual teams. I'm not aware that I ever was asked to produce any interim report. I was -- and I was producing my reports entirely independently. It was not here, it was back in my own country, so I worked on the files and produced -- sent the report. And that was it, really. So there's no pressure, other than perhaps requesting it by a certain time, no pressure for the content or any alterations in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any attempts to exert influence by various donors and sponsors, because I suppose this work involved large donations and expenses, DNA analysis and similar work requires a lot of funds. Were there any pressures exerted by those who provided the financing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you now tell us, when you worked in the mortuary, did you encounter any logistical problems that you had to deal with directly or perhaps some of your team members had to deal with?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what level of logistics you are thinking about. If it's on a level of transport or leaks coming in the ceiling or no water, yes, we had to deal with these. I imagine you are not speaking about that. Really we had -- that was not my role, but we had no major logistical issues at all. We had decent mortuary facilities, good refrigeration unit, very good co-operation from local people, and bodies arrived from the grave-site on time, so really there were no major logistic problems for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Did you encounter any problems during your work in Bosnia-Herzegovina relating to these mass graves and that kind of work?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by "problems," perhaps you'd like to explain. I think the answer will be no, but you might like to explain further.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I meant did you have any problems with the local authorities in the territories where you worked, did anybody try to disrupt your work, interfere with the crime scenes and the sites?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mortuary was -- we had absolutely no problems in the mortuary, either the security or any influence from anyone else. The mortuary was based in Visoko in Sarajevo. The field teams at the grave-sites may have had some security problems. I am aware of some problems they may have had but we certainly had no problems in the mortuary at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to know if perhaps there were some problems that impacted on the overall result and outcome of your work, the work of your team?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose the only problems were the nature of the cases we were dealing with. These were not the sort of deaths that we deal -- a forensic pathologist deals with on a daily basis. We were faced with large numbers of bodies, bodies in quite advanced states of decomposition, often unpleasant to deal with, and perhaps the mortuary facilities were not entirely of the standard that we are used to at home, but nevertheless were quite acceptable. So these were the main problems for us, but these were problems we were expecting and were able to work around within limitations, and I've explained these limitations at some length in the reports and verbally as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, for the assistance you have extended to the Defence in providing answers to questions which you did not always find clear, which you did not always understand. I wish you a safe journey home and success in your work. I have to finish my questioning here because I'm under a dead-line.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, we tried to finish within the time allocated. I have completed my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Tolimir. Ms. Chittenden, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, everyone. I do, just 15 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Good morning, again, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: I've just got maybe four short topics I'd like to ask you about before we conclude today. Firstly, yesterday you were asked a question by His Honour Judge Mindua about the possibility of injury due to trauma caused by a sharp object as opposed to a projectile trauma. Are there any distinct features in the way that these type of sharp-trauma injuries are presented?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the injuries in the bone will look different. I mean, sharp trauma could be a sharp edge striking a bone direct on to the surface, really cutting across it, in which case it will leave a nice narrow groove. Without all the fracturing 'round about it. Secondly, a sharp object could be used in a stabbing motion to penetrate through the bone and that will leave a hole which will be the shape of the large object. So if it was a knife or a bayonet it will leave the shape of that, again with very little fracturing 'round about. So for that, these are the two forms of sharp trauma which we would pick up, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Please could we have P917 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, can you tell us what type of trauma this photo shows here?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the top of the skull, looking down on it. At the top of the screen is the front of your head and down at the bottom, with the numbers, is the back of your head. So we are looking right down at the top of the skull and you have this long, horizontal defect dark area, without any fracturing 'round about it. Clearly something has gone through that skull, has penetrated right through it. It's not at all typical of a bullet because it's far too big and it's the wrong shape, and that would suggest to me that something of that shape has gone through the top of the skull. Could be various things, it could be a very broad knife. It could be a chisel, it could be a bayonet. You could think of various things it could be. But something fairly strong, well, strong to get through the bone and obviously broad to produce damage like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. If we could just look at P912, which is one of the photographs we looked at yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And just a follow-up question just before we go, can you tell if this injury was caused before or after death?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very difficult, I think. I don't think I could -- I can't confidently say it was before or after death, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, we are on to P912 now, can we -- we looked at this photo yesterday. Can you just compare that to the one we just saw?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is again is the side of the skull, the right side. Here we have the bottom left, as I explained earlier, a circular, dark hole which is highly typical of a bullet going through the skull. It's much smaller than the other damage and a different shape, and again, just to emphasise, you see the fractures coming off it in varying directions. So that's highly typical of a bullet injury.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. I've finished with that exhibit now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to the second topic. You were cross-examined extensively yesterday in relation to whether the bodies you examined could have been combat casualties. Several times you mentioned the victims at the Kozluk grave-site who had significant disabilities. I would like to show you some photographs in relation to that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If we could have P899 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, can you tell us about this photo here? Does it need to be changed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just trying to work out specifically --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Direction --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- what part -- I think that's an elbow joint. And the dark area in the middle would be your -- normally the joint, the moveable part of it. What we've got here is somebody who's had obviously an injury or perhaps infection in the past and the whole joint has become rigid, so the arm is fixed in that sort of bend. You can see the -- I think -- part of the bone, the forearm, going up the top of the screen and the upper arm up at the top. It may be the other way around. It's a little difficult to see from this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If we can turn it to the -- just so the numbers and letters are at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's actually -- it's kind of too close. It would have to be -- I mean, there must be a reference to what specific that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: That's correct. If we can see, I can point the Court, for the record, to the exhibit list which is photo showing a fixed elbow joint.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: But, can you tell us, Dr. Clark, what the effect of this type of condition would be on the person's ability to use that arm and engage in combat?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that person clearly cannot bend their elbow. Their elbow is fixed, their arm is in an angle like that, so they cannot bend their elbow or straighten their arm. It is fixed in that position. I would have thought anybody trying to fire a weapon with that disability would have great difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, I'd like to show you a second photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If we can have P900 in e-court. And if we can also just turn this one around.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Clark, can you tell us what we can see in this photo here?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a knee joint. On the left-hand side of the screen is the lower end of the femur, the thigh bone. It's been sawn off by us. And at the right-hand end is your shin bone, your tibia. The normal knee joint is in the middle. Normally the two bones would move on top of each other, here they are stuck together, and this person would have a straight leg, rigid straight leg which they could not bend their knee.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And again how would that, this condition here, affect their ability to engage in combat?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can imagine as well as I can, somebody with a straight leg, they would have difficulty in walking. It doesn't stop them fighting, but it certainly limits their ability to move around.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And from those numbers and letters we can see there, which grave is this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Kozluk, "KK" is "Kozluk," grave 3 of Kozluk, and this is the body number 820.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And is that type of finding that's consistent with what you were talking about yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: -- from that grave?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, this wasn't common. I think I've shown you probably the only two examples of that, but there were other people with abnormality of the hand, there were some people with amputations of a forearm, there was certainly one man with a glass eye, there were people with arthritis, so what I would call significant disabilities. And I've estimated about 4 per cent of the bodies in the Kozluk grave, I emphasise just Kozluk grave, had these disabilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. I have finished with that photo there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we move to another picture or document, Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Clark, I have you saying at page 13, line 13, maybe I have to -- "This is a knee joint. On the left-hand side of the screen is the lower end of the femur, the thigh bone." It's been my interest is on: "It's been sawn off by us."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the mortuary after we had examined the body, probably the -- well, maybe two reasons. Either actually to facilitate this photograph, but also in taking a DNA sample from the bone, we took it from the femur, we had to saw through the bone to take the DNA sample and so this is what we are left with here. So it's done entirely post-mortem after all the examination has been done to -- and this is what we are left with. So it's entirely sort of mortuary procedure, the cutting of the bone at either end. There's nothing more sinister in it than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't mean to say it's sinister, I just wanted to understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, just to move on to the third topic, yesterday during cross-examination you mentioned at page 5916 that in large conflicts, the characteristic injuries of victims are from explosions. My question is to you, are injuries from explosions or blasts exclusive to combat situations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: I would like to show you now if we can go to Exhibit P896.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: This is your 2000 season report.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 19, please. And these findings are in relation to the Glogova grave-site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this issue was not dealt with in cross-examination. And that's my objection. It does not arise from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Chittenden, what is your comment?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Dr. Clark, as I mentioned at page 5916, lines 1 and 2, in response to a question by the accused about the typical type of wounds caused in combat made this answer. It's a very short point that just goes back to his report, that's what it arises from. You can look at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is also my recollection, that you asked the witness about results and wounds of blasts and other explosions. Therefore, Ms. Chittenden should go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, I've just got one question. I believe on the B/C/S it's not that page. Just so the accused has the correct B/C/S page. 22 in B/C/S, please, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, if we can just have a look at the top there, as I said this is in relation to your Glogova findings. We have a heading "Blast injuries" there and we can see that you've concluded injuries caused by shrapnel were present in almost half the bodies. They were given the general term "blast injuries." We were informed they may have represented the contents of grenades, and victims had both blast and gun-shot injuries. Is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If we can just turn to page 17 in English of that report. Just should be two pages back on the B/C/S too. Page 20, B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If we can just go to paragraph 3 where it states: "We are informed there was evidence to suppose many of the bodies at Glogova were victims of the mass killing at the nearby Kravica warehouse --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down while reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Okay, sorry. I was do that with reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: "We were informed that there was evidence to suppose that many of the bodies at Glogova were the victims of a mass killing at the nearby Kravica warehouse, where it is alleged that a number of men were crammed into the building and fired on with automatic weapons and grenades." Dr. Clark, my question is: Is that finding there consistent with your conclusion you mentioned before about explosions or blast injuries not being exclusive to combat?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's entirely possible. I mean, I did make the observation yesterday that we generally had little background information to most of these graves. This was one perhaps we were given a little bit more information but not much more than I've written there. Clearly, when we started to find blast injuries in these bodies, you know, we asked questions and that this was information we were given. So certainly my findings about the finding of blast injuries and pieces of shrapnel would certainly fit with this scenario.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And just who gave you that information, just for the record?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be the investigators. I can't specify a name, but the Tribunal investigators would have passed that information on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: I've finished with that exhibit now.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Finally, Dr. Clark, I've just got one final question for you before we finish. I'd like to clarify with you one of your answers on cross-examination yesterday. It was in reference to page 10 of your 1999 season report and you were asked the following question and gave the following answer, beginning at page 5951, line 1 of the transcript. I'll read it out to be clear. The question: "You've just said that out of these 55 cases -- in these 55 cases, it was not possible to determine the cause of death. Now my question is: When it is impossible to determine the cause of death, like in these 55 cases, is it impossible for a pathologist to decide what the cause of death was and, therefore, impossible to make a reliable conclusion as to the circumstances in which that person met their death?" And your answer was: "Yes. I think, clearly, if we do not know the cause of death, it becomes very difficult to have any certainty of the circumstances of the death." Now, Dr. Clark, when you say that it is difficult to have any certainty of the circumstances of the death if we do not know the cause of the death, do you state that as a general proposition or can I take it that you are referring to the specific role and function of a forensic pathologist?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's general proposition. I mean, I could qualify that in saying that one of the reasons why we had to give unascertained for some of the bodies was there were parts missing, and it may well be that some of these parts, the missing parts, were the body parts which we looked at independently which did have gun-shot injuries in them. So I am quite willing to accept that if it was possible to associate the body part with an injury with the body, then it would be possible to come to a cause of death. So that would perhaps reduce that number, if we were able to do that. But equally, there are some cases in which we had a whole body and found no injuries, and that I think leaves it open to a variety of potential causes of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. From your answer there, I can see you're responding to cause of death and your findings of cause of death or inability to state the cause of death as a pathologist.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: My question, sorry, is slightly broader. May I give you just a hypothetical question just to put it in a bit more context. It's a different example. A plane takes off --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: -- at 9.00, it's got 300 passengers. All the passengers are alive upon takeoff.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Half an hour later, the plane crashes, bursts into flames. At the crash site, 245 of those bodies are examined by a pathologist and their cause of death is determined with certainty. So, for example, severe trauma to multiple parts of the body or organs, burns, heart attack before impact, et cetera. The other 55 bodies are also recovered from the crash site but are so charred from the flames that the pathologist cannot state with medical certainty the clinical cause of death. My question is: Does this mean that no other professional, for example, a policeman, an accident investigator, a fireman, or even an eye-witness, can state with certainty the factual circumstances surrounding how these 55 people died; that is, as a result of a plane crash?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They can state with confidence the fact that they were on the plane, were alive on the plane, and they were dead after it, and that could give very strong indications that the likelihood of dying in that incident, yes. And I think in the context of here, we still -- these bodies, the unascertained cases are still bodies who were in a mass grave and that is worth observing. I mean, I'm fully happy to accept that there may even be some people in the unascertained who have died of natural causes, I cannot exclude that, whose bodies have then been put into mass grave. I think given the overall circumstances that's possible. Which is a slightly different scenario from a plane crash, which is we know that it's observed people getting on to it, it's observed crashing, and when it comes down everyone is dead. It's a slightly more specific example than I think we have here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the doctor has answered the question in a professional manner and in keeping with his knowledge and ethics. I wanted to oppose the fact that the doctor was being given the role of an investigator, which he is not. He is an expert in his field. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Tolimir, everybody in the courtroom realised the purpose of that question, which was really hypothetical, and the doctor indeed answered that question and made it clear that there's a difference between a mass grave and a plane crash. Thank you for your comment. Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Dr. Clark, I know that your work is not an easy job and it's not a very common job either. Pathologists are hard to find. As we can see in this trial, your job is extremely important for society at large and your testimony is crucial. This is why I'm putting you a question. Yesterday, I believe the numbering has changed, but yesterday this was on page 21 of the transcript, lines 3 to 5. You mentioned the difficulties you had in seeing the bodies. You mentioned your thoughts which crossed your mind all the time while you were conducting the exhumations, or rather, the work at the hospital, at the mortuary. On today's transcript, line 7 to 9, you mentioned your thoughts and you mentioned the case of a number of deaths which were not common. Usually you examined bodies of people who had committed suicide or had died in a traffic accident. Now, this is my question: Do you think that because of these uncommon deaths, according to you, and in light of the thoughts that were crossing your mind at all times, your conclusions could be influenced one way or another, in general terms?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are correct in saying that we -- our normal work is to examine fresh bodies and we have all the facilities there. In these decomposed bodies, we try to apply the same principles of full examination of a body and looking at findings and trying to assess the significance of that. And I think -- I think we've done it very fairly and I don't think we have been biased in any huge way. I mean, naturally, as a human being, you are -- if you are told that you are dealing with bodies from a mass grave, there's an immediate assumption, but I think we can put that aside and look at all our findings very objectively. Just in the same way we have to on our routine work with a straightforward homicide in which police officers are asking us to look at things, but we've just got to stand back and look at all the evidence and assess it very impartially. So I don't think -- I think it's still possible to be completely impartial in this, and hopefully that comes over in the evidence that we provide, in indicating levels of doubt and uncertainty and where we can't come to a full answer. Not sure if that answers your question or not, but it's an attempt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask you a follow-up question. Does it happen in your normal work in Glasgow at the institute of your university that you are confronted and have to deal with decomposed bodies as well, for instance, a dead person was -- a person was missing and found later in a decomposed situation? How often does that happen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite frequent in our practice. And again, quite often we will be -- we will -- having done all the investigations, we will be saying, I don't know the answer, I don't know why this person has died. Decomposition makes various things difficult. It makes interpretation of natural disease, like in the heart or the lungs, very difficult to see. It makes toxicology, if we're thinking of alcohol or drugs, that becomes very difficult as well. So it's not uncommon that we have to give unascertained. But bear in mind, in most of these cases, what we are looking at is the soft tissues of the body, fluids and the organs of the body, and that's where the evidence lies. That's what decomposes quickly. In the bodies in the mass graves, there's still a lot of evidence from the skeleton which does remain and so that makes it -- we have the advantage of that. Most of our decomposed bodies in Glasgow will not have died from gun-shot injuries hitting the skeleton or other parts of the body which we would still see, so there's slight difference in both cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir asked you about your normal work at the University of Glasgow and the mortuary and you explained that quite extensively, but you didn't say anything about your position. What is your post, your position in this institute for forensic pathology?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we have a team of six forensic pathologists at what we call consultant level. I'm the most senior of them. I've been there the longest time. And so I'm kind of naturally the -- I have more role in administration and organisation, but I'm one of a team of six trained forensic pathologists, fully trained forensic pathologists, and the most senior one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And, indeed, thank you very much for your answers and the information you were able to provide for the Chamber. Thank you that you have come to The Hague and assisted us to find the truth. And you are now free to return to your normal activities. And like Mr. Tolimir, I wish you on behalf of the Chamber a safe journey back. Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, the next witness is ready as well. I would like to make a proposal. We should have the break, the first break now. It is easier for all arrangements. And we must have a slightly longer break today because the Chamber has to consider some duties, and therefore we have a break of 45 minutes and we'll resume quarter to 11.00. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I see you are on your feet, but before you raise some procedural matters, the Chamber would like to render an oral decision which was taken by a majority, and everybody will have realised that we have had some problems to come to a common conclusion in the Chamber. This is an oral decision on admission of evidence tendered through witness Dusan Janc. The Chamber would like to return to the pending issue on the admission of certain videos and documentary evidence that the Prosecution tendered through witness Dusan Janc on the 22nd and 23rd of September, 2010. The Chamber had marked these exhibits for identification pending a decision on admissibility. Mr. Tolimir raised some objections to the admission of some evidence. First, before turning to the merits, the Chamber wishes to clarify the applicable law and practice before the Tribunal with regard to evidence submitted to the Chamber. The Chamber, by majority, emphasises that there are two phases that should be considered in this regard. The first is the admission phase. During this phase it is sufficient for the tendering party to establish prime facie relevance and probative value of evidence and it should be admitted unless probative value is substantially overweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. However, evidence may not be admitted if obtained by methods which cast such substantial doubt on its reliability or if its admission is anti-ethical to and would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings. Yet the Chamber's decision to admit evidence is not binding upon the weight assigned to the piece of evidence during deliberations which is the second phase of evidence consideration. The decision to admit reflects no ultimate determination of the authenticity or trustworthiness of the evidence. In light of this standard, the Chamber has reviewed the witness Janc's testimony regarding the documents and videos submitted by the Prosecution and is, by majority, satisfied that they are prima facie relevant and probative under Rule 89(C) of our Rules. The Chamber is further satisfied that there are sufficient indicia and reliability present in this evidence. This finding does not prevent the Prosecution from providing more information and/or calling other witnesses who can attest to the materials in question. And this is, in fact, the question the Chamber has considered intensively and we -- on which we couldn't find a common position. The position of Judge Nyambe is that it would be much more preferable to admit some of the videos through another witness, for instance, the videographer who shot the video. Of course, he will be called by the Prosecution, as we have heard, but we can't be sure that he will appear in court at a later stage of this trial. So that is the reason why we marked several documents for identification in order to be able to identify them and to use them at a later stage and admit them at a later stage with some other witnesses. This is the position of Judge Nyambe. By majority, the Chamber has decided to admit the videos and documents tendered through witness Dusan Janc. These include Exhibit numbers P1021, P1022, P1023, P1024, P1027, P1025, I forgot that. P1028, P1029, and the document 65 ter number 6576. That was the decision of the Chamber and now, Mr. McCloskey, if you want to raise another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. And we will, of course, endeavour to bring the videographer and we'll keep you informed on our efforts to do that. And he has testified in Serbia and we will obtain a certified copy of that transcript, but we will endeavour to bring him here with all the power of the Court and our ability to do so. And that, of course, is true of any other witness that you think is appropriate. We can't always -- that one we know we need to get for you. And we will try to anticipate all the others that you may need, but of course, we will endeavour to bring anyone that you think -- well, of course, you, as you know, have the absolute power to bring whoever you would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And, Mr. McCloskey, may I interrupt you. The Chamber would appreciate that, and this not only by majority, but all members of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely. On the similar subject, today Ms. Gallagher, who has always been scheduled to testify about two basic exhibits, one is the trial video which I think you've seen a fair amount of, we played part of it through Mr. Ruez, the sort of chronologic video of Srebrenica and other things, and specifically a book of stills that we have made based on that video so that when you see the video, you can see who the Prosecution feels the various people are, so that it makes some sense. It's a lot of video, it's a lot of material, it's going to require your viewing a few times. However, we have -- we'll bring the -- the key witnesses that are in this video we hope to bring to you as the most significant evidence. But Ms. Gallagher will give you our best efforts on where the video came from, where we got it, those sort of basic things, plus she will go through the video book and explain the identifications that were made. Much of this, of course, is -- are hearsay identifications of the investigations. And -- but to try to clear up a matter, the video -- the trial video is P991, and Ms. Stewart tells me that that came into evidence through Mr. Kingori on e-court. However, Mr. Kingori only testified, as you recall, about a few clips, mostly that he was in or that he was part of. And the trial video is much more immense than that. And so we don't -- never expected that the entire video would have come in. I don't know if that's the way it looks on e-court, but that's not necessary now for it to be in. One of the reasons I say that is because what we want to provide to you is a complete trial video based on the new material that Mr. Janc was speaking about and that we got relatively recently, so we don't need that video in evidence right now. We want to provide you the complete version as we finish doing the editing and putting it together and so you have a complete -- a complete video that we can provide you on DVDs as well so you are not having to search in e-court for the various pieces. As well, we'll have a new book of people that are in the video that will go along with it. But it's my intention today to play parts of the -- the old video so that you can see where we are getting pieces from and she can help you identify various people in it and use the old -- well, pictures from the old book because it will also help identify the video. And the video and the book are, I'm not sure, 80 per cent the same than the new material, but with new material we want to give you a package that's complete and we should be able do that in the next month or so as -- well, we now especially since we see that -- we didn't want to put anything in a book that wasn't into evidence. So now that there are things into evidence, we can put a more complete picture for you. And I just wanted to let you know that. So I'll be dealing with these two P numbers, the book, P624, and the trial video, P991, and be asking the witness about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If there's nothing else to address the Chamber with, the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Ms. Stewart will be working the video and the Registrar will be working the stills book and we'll hope things will go smoothly as they have, but we'll give it our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm sure, and there are so many experienced people in the courtroom, it will be managed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Gallagher. Welcome to the Tribunal. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now please sit down. Mr. McCloskey for the Prosecution has questions for you. Just a moment. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one technical remark. Since Mr. McCloskey and the witness speak the same language, the transcript -- in fact, the Serbian interpretation lags sometimes as much as two paragraphs behind the transcript. And Mr. Tolimir sometimes has difficulty, he is still listening to the interpretation of testimony, for instance, when you have already started speaking, Mr. President. I would therefore, appreciate if Mr. McCloskey and the witness would make a short pause before questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that advice, it's indeed very helpful. That is always the problem if counsel and witness speak the same language, and I hope very much that Mr. McCloskey and the witness will take that into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. You'd think after 12 years I would have had that figured out, but I do, as you know, as probably as early as a couple of days ago, do that. We will try our best, of course, and do that. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: It's Erin Gallagher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is your position?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: I'm an investigator with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what case have you been assigned to?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: I've been assigned to the Srebrenica case, to both Popovic and to now the Tolimir case in trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Have you ever testified here before?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: No, this is my first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We do need to, both of us, keep in mind this delay. And one good thing to -- if you can look at the -- sometimes looking at the screen will help, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not the only indicator because the translation into B/C/S you can't see on the screen, so please be even more patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The trouble is the longer I wait the more my mind goes somewhere else. But we'll get a good rhythm going and we'll be able to do this. Can you tell us how long you have worked as an investigator for the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: I've worked for the OTP for a little over four and a half years now. I arrived in January 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And has -- have you worked on the same Srebrenica case that entire time?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And before we go into a little more detail about your work as an investigator, let's hear a bit more about yourself. Where were you born and raised?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: I was born in the US. I spent much of my last -- at least the last 20 years in San Francisco, California.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us your educational levels?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: I went to college, to university, the University of Wisconsin and did my bachelor's degree there and then I did a master's degree at San Francisco State University.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what you majored in, what your bachelor major was?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: My bachelor's was in international relations, Russian studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And your master's?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: And my master's was in gender studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you get your master's degree, what year?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: That was in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you do after getting your master's in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: Shortly thereafter I actually joined the San Francisco police department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you describe, just briefly, your career there, what kind of training you had, for how long, and what kind of assignments you had?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: I went to the police academy for six months, my first six months in training, and then worked as a police officer on the streets for two years after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: Then I transferred to the district attorney's office and worked as an investigator for that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you can you tell us what a district attorney's office is?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: It's the -- the prosecutor for crimes in the city and county of San Francisco.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you just briefly describe how an investigator's job may differ from the prosecutor's office than it would the police department?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: Generally, the police department, the detective inspector in a police department will do the immediate investigation. They will do immediately from the arrest or up until the arrest and then oftentimes the district attorney's office will take over the investigation after the arrest and prior to the trial. At the same time there are cases that the district attorney's office will investigate right from the start, and will keep the case, the investigation, through to the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how many years did you work as a DA, as they call it, DA's investigator?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: I worked there for eight years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you give us just a few examples of your most significant investigations?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: I worked many of the violent crimes that came through San Francisco, through the office. I worked a -- was a cold case homicide, a murder case that was 15 years old. I worked a serial rape case, a number of serial rape cases, a number of rape cases, sexual assault cases. I also worked a number of child abuse cases. Those were predominantly the areas that I worked when I was with the district attorney's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And after your eight years there, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: Then I came to the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember the month and year?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: I arrived here January 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us a little bit about the investigative -- your investigative work here. Let's start with who else was in your investigative team for the Srebrenica case?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: When I first arrived, it was a little bit of a time of transition. The prior investigator, Bruce Bursik, was leaving so we did not overlap very much at all. And then shortly thereafter, Investigator Tomasz Blaszczyk came back on to the team, and then not long after, another investigator, Dusan Janc also joined the team. So it was the three of us very early on in 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that the current makeup of the team?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: Those are the investigators. Certainly the team encompasses analysts, interpreters, you know, attorneys, so it's a larger team than obviously just the three of us investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And have you had any particular assignments or been given any particular areas to focus on?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: It's been quite varied since I've been here. One part of the investigation that I did work quite a bit on was the Kravica execution and the events around Kravica. Otherwise some of the areas that I've spent a bit of time on are some of the forensic analysis or work or consulting with forensic experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about anything to do with the Ministry of Interior police forces?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: And that's part of the Kravica execution. It's the MUP forces that were in the area at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And how about anything related to the video and the stills book that came out of what we all have been referring to as the Srebrenica trial video?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: And certainly as part of the investigation as well as assisting with the trials and trial exhibits is working with what we call the stills book, the photo book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the record, the stills book is P624 and the trial video I speak of is P991. And there is a transcript of the trial video in e-court which is P008. Sorry, P1008.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in fact, were you prepared to testify about the stills book in the previous trial, the Popovic trial?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you in fact testify?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: No. At the time there was a stipulation by the Defence to the book and I ended up not having to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to the subject matter of your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Unless there's any other questions, of course, feel free to interrupt us at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you managed to view in part and study the Srebrenica trial video, P991?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what have you -- what has your study in preparation for your testimony today -- what have you looked into? Just give us a rough idea, we'll go into some details.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: Of course part of it is viewing the video many times. Also looking at the original footage, the raw footage that made up the trial video. Looking at researching where we got some of that original material, and also speaking with the film-maker who made the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And the Trial Chamber has seen portions of it, large portions, through Jean-Rene, that was a long time ago, and through others, so I don't think we need to describe that too much. But can you tell us what you've learned about how this trial video, this series of shots from south of Srebrenica, Srebrenica, Potocari and on, how that was assembled?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: The film-maker as well as the investigators that were working on the case at that time compiled numerous videos that were in-house at the ICTY and assisted in -- the investigators assisted the film-maker with what the videos were, anything that was related to Srebrenica, to the Srebrenica operation, and she, the film-maker, Marta Fracassetti, viewed all the footage that existed at the Tribunal and started compiling some rough edits of the video and working closely with the investigators and I think the trial attorneys at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, when you say Ms. Fracassetti looked at all the video of the Tribunal, is that correct or was she looking in a particular area?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: She was looking at all videos that were related to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us just a little bit about how it was that Ms. Fracassetti was working on this project?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: She was hired to make this video, employed to make this video at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know when she worked doing this job?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: This was from 2002 to 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us where she's working today?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: She works in the audio-visual unit for the courtrooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so --

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: Here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So she began with the Office of the Prosecutor and then what?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: And then she started working for, which I believe is the Registry, the audio-visual unit here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And when did you have a chance to speak with her about the process that she used?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: I spoke with her a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you just tell us roughly what her mandate was and what she did in looking at all these videos?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: Her mandate was to create a video that was as complete and full and accurate that told the story of Srebrenica with the footage that we had, and her focus was to use the most complete footage, video footage that existed, as well as the best quality footage that existed, so to make the best quality video they actually could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But who was actually directing the overall substance of it?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: The content was directed mainly by the investigators on the team at that time, as well as input from the attorneys.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you say the most complete, do you know if she actually edited any segments of it or was it everything that the Srebrenica video collection had, or a combination thereof?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: It is actually a combination, obviously she couldn't put in all the footage for all of us to watch for days so she had to make edits. And some of the footage that existed at the Tribunal also was, you know, in duplicate form too. There are some portions that she put in in its entirety, some portions of the video, and some other portions that she had to edit and using the best quality of the video that existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We may get into a little more detail on that as we go through some of it, and of course, Ms. Fracassetti is available if anything more particular is needed. All right. So tell us about your job, your mandate in relation to this stills book, P624, and the trial video?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: Well, the stills book parallels the video. The stills book is comprised of photographs that are captured from the video. So everything that is in the stills book is from the trial video. Over time I've added photographs from the videos myself in to it, but for the most part, it was already a pre-existing book that was made years ago. So I've certainly familiarised myself with the stills book at the same time as watching the trial video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is the trial video and the stills book, are they both still works in progress?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: They are. They are. We -- though the stills book has for the most part remained the same for many years. In the last couple of years we had received new -- last year, I should say, we received new video footage and so we would like to add more photographs from the recent videos. And also as -- over the course of when I have been reviewing the book and reviewing the videos, I'm noticing some things that I think should be changed, we think should be changed and some corrections. There are some small mistakes in it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Have you had a chance to look at most of the -- or actually identify, not look at, but actually identify the various sources of video that Ms. Fracassetti used in compiling and editing and making this product?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: Yes. And not only have I viewed the entire video numerous times, I've also looked at the underlying original footage used within the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go through, well, most of or some of to give the Court an idea of the kinds of sources she was using, and if you can do it in the time-frame chronologically of when we received the material at the OTP, that would be helpful. If not, then just give us an idea of what it is the OTP got and when we received it.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: Right. We've gotten videos from a number of different sources spanning many years. The -- some of the first Srebrenica-related video that I know that we've received was actually early, it was in December of 1995, and that was received by Jean-Rene Ruez when he was in Sarajevo, when he received it directly from the police in Sarajevo in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what roughly did this video he received contain?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: It was footage of the approach to Srebrenica and entry into Srebrenica. Much of it -- in fact, I think all of it is from the -- what is called SRT, Srpska Radio Television station, and it was footage that you can see was broadcast on SRT in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how are you able to make that conclusion, that it was broadcast?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: You will see the SRT logo on the footage. You'll notice it in the trial video, you'll see it's in Cyrillic, looks like CPT, but SRT in the upper corner, upper right corner or upper left corner of the video footage. So that I believe is the first, the earliest footage we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us a brief idea of -- I mean, obviously you were not here in 1995. What sorts of investigation or review, what have you looked at to determine these basics of when we receive things and from who? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: Well, each video as well as every document that comes through will -- comes through the Tribunal is placed into our evidence unit. It's given an evidence number and therefore there's a trail, a record of when it arrived and on that record -- and it's called a MIF, mini-indexing information form, will be some information of when it was received, who it was received by, where, and the date. So that's generally the first place to look. In addition, we may find that there have been requests, letters. There may be some correspondence, RFAs, request for assistance, that can also provide a record of when videos arrived to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So this material, this Serb television, Serb radio and television material that was provided by, I think you said the Sarajevo police, would this be the Bosnia and Herzegovina Muslim side of the world back in those days, or would it have been the Republika Srpska Sarajevo police?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: This particular footage from 1995 came from the Bosnia-Herzegovina Muslim side and specifically came from the Centre for Security Services.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that known as AID?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, the CSB. Okay. All right. And do you know from the records or did you find out, you know, how the Muslim police obtained this footage that appears to be from Serb radio and television?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: From the record it gives me limited information of where and when it was received. I fortunately work with the interpreter who happened to be there at the time with Mr. -- with Investigator Ruez and she actually remembered picking up the video footage during a mission in December of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any information on how the -- how the Muslim police actually got this footage?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: It was broadcast on SRT during that time-period and they taped it off of the TV and the tapes arrived in a VHS format.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. What other source of video did we get that found its way into the trial video?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: And I'll still try and keep it chronological. In 1998 we received directly from SRT, Srpska Radio Television, footage, and that was also a mission with analysts who were collecting documents and at the same time collected video footage from SRT in -- which is located in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. What else?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: 1999, we received quite a bit of footage, you'll see on the trial video, that is from Antelope Productions and that was a production company that made a documentary called "A Cry From the Grave" which was then aired on the BBC. And we have requested, meaning the team at that time, requested all the raw footage that made up their documentary, "A Cry From the Grave." So in 1999, December 1st, 1999, they gave us all of their raw footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you able to determine where they got their raw footage, and I mean not their, you know, their movie side of things but the raw footage that was alleged to be real-time event-related footage?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: They did give us a tape log that listed all of their footage. It did include their own footage, you know, that they taped in 1999, but it also included what would be archival footage, where they got footage from 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you give us some examples of where they got their material or where at least they say they got it in their -- in this index you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: They received some of their footage from archives, such as Pale archives --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do -- sorry, do you know what that was a reference to?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: No, actually, I just have limited information. I would only presume what it might be, but I actually don't know. It's fairly limited what they gave us in terms of description of where they got their original sources. They also received footage from archives in Tuzla. I know they received footage from the archives at the BBC, from the Tribunal, from United Nations. They received footage from individuals as well, individuals that were there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, there's a part of the trial video, I think the Court has seen it, that shows mostly men walking through meadows and woods in a path, and we'll get to that a little bit later, but was -- where did we get that from?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: The footage that you are talking about does come from Antelope Productions. It is from their original source. We don't know who that person is. They haven't identified them, but you will see from the footage that it is a, you know, somebody that was -- who was in the column, a Muslim who was in the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we may get a little bit more into that or we will when we get to that segment of the video. Anything else in the -- that they pointed us to in their index of where they got material?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: They did also receive material from the Dutch authorities, from DutchBat individuals who were in Srebrenica in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Aside from reviewing their index, have you been able to reach anyone or get any further information on, you know, more detail about where these journalists, movie-makers got their sources?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: No, not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Aside from Antelope Productions, where else did we get material?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: We received a large portion of material as well from the BBC in the year 2000. And if I can add that the footage that we got from the BBC, they also noted to us that they had gotten some of their raw footage from WTN, World Television Network, and from Reuters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And tell us what WTN is?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: World Television Network, it's a -- my understanding basically like a clearing house like Reuters. They sell raw footage to network stations around the world, and such as the BBC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Any other -- what are the other sources, anything else? We may as -- how about did the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has heard about some new sources of video from Dusan Janc, but not counting those that Mr. Janc has mentioned, are there any other sources that you can recall right now that you may have?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: There's another large portion of the trial video that you'll see that is made up of video footage from Zoran Petrovic. We often refer to it as the Petrovic video. And that will cover from July -- mainly the day of July 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We'll talk a little bit more about that when we get there. I notice that you've got some materials in front of you. Can you just tell us what they are so we know what you might be using?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: Well, I have the stills book that you have in front of you as well, and then at the same time there is an index that is -- basically it's a list of all the sources that were used in the making of the trial video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I see a little blue book underneath that?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: And this is a -- it is the MIFs, the MIF forms of the sources, of the videos.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if you need to review any of that material to answer, that's fine, just let us know you are doing it so that is clear. And in the book itself, the trial -- the stills book, have you made any of your own little notes in there that won't be on the version that was provided to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: I have. In the places where it says that somebody has testified in trial, I've just noted in pencil for myself the dates that they testified just to give a more exact day of when they identified the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you make those notations?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: In the course of the last couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the index that she's referred to is 65 ter 1451.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think we'll get started pretty quickly, but can you tell us before we do just a little bit more about how the layout of the stills book worked for any given still. What information aside from the still is on there and why?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: You'll see that the stills book follows chronologically the video. It's not a hundred per cent accurate. There may be a scene or two that's out of order, and within each still, there will be the person or sometimes the vehicle that's identified from the video, as well as who identifies them or how they are identified. And in addition to that, there will be the site of the video source, the original video source, and our evidence number of that video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And in the making of the editing of the trial video, was there an attempt to make this in some kind of chronology?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
utterances.text: Correct. It was done as best as possible to keep it chronologically accurate, both the video and the stills book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Having seen it and studied it, in your view was it always possible to get the chronology just right?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER
